title: Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others
lead: A securities agent cultivates customers who later obtain placements without commissions or through other channels. He asks the court to imply duties preventing the brokerage from competing for those transactions.

actors.name: Ng Giap Hon
actors.role: Self-employed remisier and contractual agent of Westcomb Securities.

actors.name: Westcomb Securities
actors.role: Brokerage principal owing a percentage of commissions charged on transactions through Ng.

actors.name: Westcomb Financial Group and Westcomb Capital
actors.role: Listed parent and corporate-finance affiliate sued with the brokerage.

actors.name: Tan Kah Koon and another senior group officer
actors.role: Individual conspiracy defendants; Tan also directed the brokerage.

actors.name: Julian Sandt, Orchid Emarb and Aktieninvestor
actors.role: Individual and corporate customers whose different accounts and placements were central.

proceedings: The High Court separated liability and quantum and dismissed at the liability stage.
The Court of Appeal rejected the entire-agreement bar as applied but declined both implied terms and agreed on custom and conspiracy findings.
The appeal was dismissed with costs and usual consequential orders on April 29, 2009.
limits: This source-brief account uses the full judgment’s chronology and paragraph numbers, without a new audit or current comparative-law claim. It distinguishes disputed customer-origin claims from account records and alleged conspiracy from findings. Deliberate systematic sabotage and vested commission situations were reserved, not authorized. Later editorial cases are not 2009 authorities.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Ng’s agreement defines the commission he can earn
sections.cue: What relationship and payment trigger did the writing create?
paragraphs: Ng Giap Hon was a remisier, a self-employed securities trader associated with a brokerage. Although remisiers cultivated customers they regarded as their own, Ng’s May 3, 2005 agreement made him Westcomb Securities’ agent, not its employee. Westcomb Securities belonged to a group including listed parent Westcomb Financial Group and corporate-finance company Westcomb Capital. Two senior officers were also later defendants; Tan Kah Koon was a brokerage director.

Ng would receive forty percent of the brokerage’s commission on transactions dealt by or through him for the first year and fifty percent thereafter. The percentage applied to commission actually charged, not share purchase price. Clause 12 denied employment. Clause 18 expressed the entire understanding, disclaimed outside oral, written, express or implied obligations, and preserved accrued rights under earlier agreements. No express term granted customer exclusivity or required commission on every transaction.

sections.title: Sandt’s contacts develop into several different accounts and placements
sections.cue: Which transactions actually passed through Ng?
paragraphs: Ng said he met Orchid Capital chief executive Julian Sandt at a February 2006 networking event and generated interest in initial-public-offering placement shares for Sandt and connected companies. Defendants disputed that origin, pointing to earlier group relationships and pre-IPO discussions. The established account sequence was narrower: Sandt opened an individual account through Ng around March 6, and Orchid Capital subsidiary Orchid Emarb opened its account through him March 15.

On April 27, Sandt subscribed for 1.5 million Natural Cool placement shares at $0.20, totaling $300,000, without a brokerage commission. That day connected Austrian company Aktieninvestor separately agreed to buy 7.8 million shares in Westcomb’s parent. Another broker arranged that transaction and earned $85,000.

Ng said he arranged a May placement meeting and sent Aktieninvestor account forms. Later emails showed its chief executive sent them to Tan at Tan’s request; the chief executive could not recall why and suggested Ng might have been away. A group officer said Sandt and overseas secondary listings were too important or large for Ng. Aktieninvestor opened its account May 29 without Ng and received a firm dealer.

In October Aktieninvestor subscribed for 1.5 million Swiber shares through Australian broker BBY, while Sandt bought 750,000 at $0.355, totaling $266,250. Neither transaction carried commission. Orchid Emarb bought no placement shares, and Ng received his contractual commission on its ordinary trades through him. These were not all completed commission-earning transactions for Ng merely because the customers were connected.

sections.title: The High Court rejects custom, conspiracy and implied duties
paragraphs: Ng sued the brokerage under its agency agreement and alleged that the other four defendants conspired to deprive him of commissions. The High Court bifurcated liability and quantum and dismissed at liability. It found no reliable proof of the alleged customary one-percent placement commission, no obligation to charge when shares were allocated as goodwill, and no coherent proved conspiracy. It partly relied on the entire-agreement clause against implied good faith and rejected a poorly developed quantum-meruit theory.

On appeal Ng sought a general good-faith duty between principal and agent and a narrower obligation that the brokerage do nothing to deprive him of earning commission. The Court of Appeal agreed with the custom and conspiracy findings, and Ng abandoned quantum meruit. It therefore examined whether clause 18 barred implication and whether either proposed term satisfied the appropriate test.

sections.title: The clause does not foreclose implication, but necessity still limits it
sections.cue: Why did rejecting the threshold bar not establish the requested protection?
paragraphs: Andrew Phang delivered the judgment for Chao Hick Tin, Phang and V. K. Rajah. This clause’s own reference to implied terms contemplated their existence and did not bar implication. The court did not extend that result to every entire-agreement clause: clear language could exclude implied terms, subject to common-law controls and the Unfair Contract Terms Act if it functioned as an exclusion clause. No implied term could contradict an express one.

A term implied in fact fills a necessary gap in the particular agreement according to presumed intention. Business efficacy and the officious-bystander inquiry complemented each other: would both parties unhesitatingly agree because the term was necessary? Fairness or desirability alone was insufficient. A term implied in law instead applies on broader policy grounds to a class of contracts and carries wider future consequences.

The court declined a general good-faith term in law. The examined 2009 authorities disagreed about honesty, commercial fair dealing, exclusion of bad faith, recapturing surrendered opportunities, and whether good faith belonged in a separate term or existing doctrines. That uncertainty counseled against the broad class-wide duty proposed. It did not legalize dishonesty or deny particular statutory good-faith obligations.

sections.title: The actual commission bargain does not require exclusivity
sections.cue: Why did Luxor’s exceptional protections not resolve Ng’s case?
paragraphs: The rejection of general good faith left room for fact-specific protection if necessary. The court used Luxor v. Cooper to examine risk allocation and the exact event earning commission, not to impose a universal commission rule. Protection could arise when the agent had done everything required and the principal refused a binding transaction, wrongfully prevented the agent’s contractual performance, or expressly accepted exclusivity.

Here the brokerage retained discretion to allocate placements directly and waive charges; its trading conditions expressly allowed waivers. It could deal with important customers, and customers could keep multiple accounts and use different dealers. Sandt said he did not intend the disputed placements through Ng. Aktieninvestor’s Swiber purchase used BBY rather than any brokerage account, while Orchid Emarb’s actual Ng trades generated his payment.

Introducing a customer or having forms redirected did not establish entitlement to every later placement. The requested duty would substantially surrender discretion neither the agreement nor customer intentions had surrendered. The agreement already worked by linking payment to transactions through Ng and commission charged; both parties would not necessarily have accepted the broader restriction at formation.

The court expressed sympathy and suggested a voluntary compromise might be fairer, but could not impose it. On April 29, 2009, it dismissed with costs and the usual consequential orders, with no separate opinion. It reserved different facts such as deliberate systematic sabotage that might require a protective term in fact and perhaps law. The ruling did not permit sabotage or cancellation of vested rights. The complete judgment’s May account date and BBY route control over compressed editorial discrepancies, and later references to Wastech, Braganza and Yam Seng remain later context.
